text:
2. Model specification
The marginal model is \[
Y_i\sim N\{X_i\beta,\Sigma_i(\theta)\}.
\] Examples include CS, \(\Sigma_{jk}=\sigma^2\{(1-\rho)I(j=k)+\rho\}\); discrete AR(1), \(\Sigma_{jk}=\sigma^2\rho^{|j-k|}\); continuous AR(1), \(\sigma^2\rho^{|t_j-t_k|}\); Toeplitz, \(\Sigma_{jk}=\sigma^2\rho_{|j-k|}\); and unstructured \(\Sigma\).
The LMM is \[
Y_i=X_i\beta+Z_i b_i+\varepsilon_i,qquad
b_i\sim N(0,D),\quad \varepsilon_i\sim N(0,R_i),\quad b_i\perp\varepsilon_i,
\] so \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=Z_iDZ_i^{\mathsf T}+R_i\) and \[
\widehat b_i=DZ_i^{\mathsf T}V_i^{-1}(Y_i-X_i\widehat\beta).
\]

Random-intercept and random-slope variances quantify unexplained between-subject heterogeneity; their correlation describes association between baseline level and change. title: 3. Gaussian covariance models and linear mixed models
text:
8. Caveats

Compare fixed-effect mean structures under ML. REML likelihoods from different fixed-effect column spaces are not comparable; compare covariance/random-effect structures under REML only with the same fixed effects.
LRTs are justified for nested models; AIC/BIC may compare nonnested covariance structures but do not account for selection uncertainty.
For a single variance component under a regular scalar boundary problem, the asymptotic null is \(\tfrac12\chi_0^2+\tfrac12\chi_1^2\), not plain \(\chi_1^2\). Multiple components or unidentified correlations require a different mixture or parametric bootstrap.
SAS PROC MIXED often requests DDFM=KR or DDFM=SAT; base lmer() supplies neither automatically. lmerTest defaults to Satterthwaite unless changed.
Wald CIs for variance parameters are unreliable near zero; prefer profile-likelihood or bootstrap intervals.
nlme::corCAR1() and corExp() use actual time distances; corAR1() uses integer occasion gaps.
nlme does not natively expose unrestricted Toeplitz covariance; the glmmTMB homogeneous Toeplitz term homtoep() is an explicit R-vs-SAS implementation difference. Use toep() when occasion-specific marginal variances are required.
Multilevel random effects require enough independent levels at each hierarchy; a factor with only a few levels should ordinarily be fixed. Nonlinear mixed models are sensitive to starting values and parameterization.
Source-backed: model-building order, covariance choices, REML/ML, boundary tests, BLUPs, and diagnostics follow the source notes. Standard-practice additions: broom.mixed, influence.ME, and glmmTMB Toeplitz syntax replace or extend SAS output.

title: A1. Inference and diagnostics
text:
2. Model specification
For an LMM, marginal residuals are \(r_i^{(m)}=Y_i-X_i\widehat\beta\) and conditional residuals are \(r_i^{(c)}=Y_i-X_i\widehat\beta-Z_i\widehat b_i\). For GLM/GLMM mean \(\widehat\mu\), Pearson residuals are \((Y-\widehat\mu)/\sqrt{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(Y)}\); deviance residuals are signed square roots of unit-deviance contributions. Cluster influence compares \(\widehat\beta\) with \(\widehat\beta_{(-i)}\).

title: A1. Inference and diagnostics
text:
8. Caveats

Marginal residuals retain random-effect variation; conditional residuals depend on estimated BLUPs and can mask random-effect misspecification.
QQ plots of BLUPs do not directly test the latent random-effects distribution because BLUPs are heteroscedastic, correlated, and shrunken.
Pearson/deviance residuals are discrete and nonnormal in GLMMs; simulation-based residuals are usually more interpretable.
Cook’s distance and DFBETAs should be deleted by independent cluster, not by row, for longitudinal data.
A flat residual variogram is evidence against remaining second-order lag structure only after the mean and random effects are adequate.
Singularity is a boundary estimate, not an optimizer failure; convergence warnings require gradient/Hessian and rescaling checks before changing optimizers.
SAS PROC MIXED influence measures and R package measures can use different scaling; compare rankings and deleted estimates, not labels alone.
Source-backed: residual taxonomy, variograms, and influence follow BIOS 767/STAT 571. Standard-practice addition: DHARMa, performance, and influence.ME provide native R diagnostics.

text:
2. Model specification
For group \(g\), subject \(i\), and occasion \(j\), \[
Y_{gij}=\mu+\alpha_g+\tau_j+(\alpha\tau)_{gj}+u_{gi}+e_{gij}.
\] The univariate F test for within-subject effects requires \(C\Sigma C^{\mathsf T}=\sigma^2 I\) for an orthonormal within-subject contrast matrix \(C\). Profile hypotheses are \[
H_{\mathrm{parallel}}:C\mu_1=\cdots=C\mu_G,\quad
H_{\mathrm{coincident}}:\mu_1=\cdots=\mu_G,\quad
H_{\mathrm{flat}}:C\bar\mu=0.
\]

Repeated-measures sample size from a planned contrast
For two equally allocated groups and planned contrast \(c\), a normal-approximation calculation uses \(\operatorname{Var}(c^{\mathsf T}\bar Y_1-c^{\mathsf T}\bar Y_0)=4c^{\mathsf T}\Sigma c/N\), where \(N\) is total sample size.

Sigma_plan <- stats::cov(Y)
c_change <- c(-1, 0, 0, 1)            # age-14 minus age-8 change
delta <- 2                              # target difference in mean changes
alpha <- 0.05
power <- 0.80
N_total <- ceiling(
  4 * drop(t(c_change) %*% Sigma_plan %*% c_change) *
    (qnorm(1 - alpha / 2) + qnorm(power))^2 / delta^2
)
N_total + (N_total %% 2)                # enforce equal allocation

6. Extract & interpret
The Sex:age_f test is the parallelism test; if rejected, report time-specific or change-specific contrasts rather than an average sex effect. Conditional on parallelism, the Sex test addresses coincidence and the age_f test addresses flatness. Greenhouse–Geisser and Huynh–Feldt results alter numerator/denominator degrees of freedom, whereas multivariate Pillai/Wilks tests do not impose sphericity.

title: 2. Repeated-measures ANOVA, MANOVA, and profile analysis
text:
8. Caveats

Base aov() uses sequential sums of squares; term order matters in unbalanced designs. car::Anova(type = 3) requires deliberate contrasts and estimability checks.
A nonsignificant interaction does not mechanically require refitting before Type III main-effect tests; interpretations remain conditional on the chosen contrast coding.
MANOVA avoids sphericity but is complete-case and becomes unstable as the response dimension approaches the number of independent subjects.
emmeans contrasts from gls use the fitted covariance model and are the idiomatic R analogue of SAS ESTIMATE/CONTRAST statements.
Source-backed: RM-ANOVA/MANOVA hypotheses and profile sequence are from BIOS 767. Standard-practice addition: the car and emmeans implementations replace SAS GLM/MIXED syntax.

title: 5. GLM review for longitudinal outcomes
text:
2. Model specification
For an exponential-family response, \[
f(y;\theta,\phi)=\exp\left\{\frac{y\theta-b(\theta)}{a(\phi)}+c(y,\phi)\right\},
\quad E(Y)=b'(\theta),\quad \operatorname{Var}(Y)=a(\phi)b''(\theta),
\] and a GLM sets \(g(\mu_{ij})=x_{ij}^{\mathsf T}\beta+\log(e_{ij})\), where \(e_{ij}\) is exposure for a log-link rate model. Common longitudinal outcomes use binomial-logit, Poisson-log, negative-binomial-log, or Gaussian-identity specifications.

Exponentiated log-link coefficients are conditional rate ratios under the fitted mean model; the offset converts expected counts to rates per exposure unit. title: 5. GLM review for longitudinal outcomes
text:
8. Caveats

These fits ignore repeated-subject correlation; use GEE for population-average inference or GLMM for a conditional random-effects model.
Pearson/deviance dispersion ratios are screens, not formal universal tests, and repeated dependence itself inflates them.
Quasi-likelihood models have no ordinary likelihood; do not compare their AIC with likelihood fits.
Exponentiation is link-specific: odds ratios for logit, rate ratios for log, and no ratio interpretation for identity.
Wald inference may be unreliable with sparse outcomes, boundary estimates, or separation; use likelihood or penalized methods as appropriate.
Proportional-odds coefficients assume common covariate effects across cumulative logits; assess this constraint before reporting a single ordinal odds ratio. Nominal multinomial models require a separate set of logits and a dependence strategy.
Source-backed: family/link, likelihood, offsets, Wald/LRT, interactions, and overdispersion are in the notes. Standard-practice addition: MASS::glm.nb() is the idiomatic R extension for overdispersed counts.

Quantity
Concise interpretation




LMM fixed intercept
Expected response for the reference covariate pattern at the time origin; recenter time if this is extrapolative.


LMM fixed slope
Expected response change per time unit for the reference group; with an interaction it is not the common slope.


Group x time
Difference in time slopes (continuous time) or difference of occasion contrasts (factor time).


Random-intercept variance
Residual between-subject heterogeneity in the conditional intercept.


Random-slope variance
Residual between-subject heterogeneity in conditional change; marginal variance/correlation then depends on time.


Random-effect correlation
Association between latent deviations; inspect time centering because it changes the intercept and its correlation with slope.


BLUP/conditional mode
Shrunken subject deviation conditional on the fitted population model and variance parameters.


Random-intercept ICC
\(\tau_0^2/(\tau_0^2+\sigma^2)\) for the Gaussian random-intercept model only.


GEE coefficient
Population-average change in the link of the marginal mean.


GEE working \(\alpha\)
Nuisance association parameter used for efficiency; not generally a target unless association is explicitly modeled.


GEE robust SE
Sandwich uncertainty, asymptotically robust to working-correlation misspecification.


GEE model-based SE
Valid only if the working covariance is correctly specified.


GEE scale \(\phi\)
Marginal variance multiplier under the package’s scale-estimation rule.


Logistic GLMM \(e^{\beta}\)
Subject-specific conditional odds ratio at equal random effects.


Logistic GEE \(e^{\beta}\)
Population-average marginal odds ratio.


Poisson/log GLMM \(e^{\beta}\)
Conditional rate ratio; an offset fixes the exposure denominator.


Satterthwaite/KR df
Approximate denominator df for a specified fixed-effect test; KR also adjusts covariance/test statistic.

3. R packages/functions

Data manipulation and visualization

dplyr — long-format grouping, summaries, joins, and creation of subject/time variables.
tidyr — wide-to-long reshaping with pivot_longer() and balanced-grid construction with complete().
ggplot2 — individual profiles, mean-profile plots, residual displays, and diagnostic graphics.
naniar — missingness summaries and pattern visualizations such as vis_miss() and gg_miss_upset().



Gaussian repeated measures and linear mixed models

nlme — gls()/lme() models with explicit residual covariance structures, including CS, AR(1), continuous-time AR(1), spatial correlation, and unstructured correlation.
lme4 — sparse, modular fitting of linear and generalized linear mixed models via lmer() and glmer().
lmerTest — Satterthwaite or Kenward–Roger denominator-df tests for lmer() fixed effects.
pbkrtest — Kenward–Roger and parametric-bootstrap comparisons for nested Gaussian mixed models.



Marginal models and GEE

geepack — geeglm() GEE fitting, robust/model-based covariance extraction, common working correlations, and QIC via QIC().
gee — alternative GEE implementation whose summary exposes naive and robust standard errors and scale estimation directly.



Generalized linear mixed models

lme4 — Laplace or adaptive Gauss–Hermite fitting of standard-family GLMMs through glmer(..., nAGQ=).
glmmTMB — flexible GLMMs with offsets, zero inflation, dispersion models, and families such as negative binomial and beta-binomial.



Missing data and weighting

mice — multiple imputation by chained equations, passive transformations, multilevel imputation methods, and Rubin pooling.
mitools — manipulation and pooling of multiply imputed analyses when model-specific mice::pool() support is unavailable.
WeightIt — construction and diagnostics of inverse-probability weights; longitudinal dropout weights usually require explicit visit-specific models.
survey — weighted estimating-equation analyses with design-aware sandwich variance estimation.



Contrasts, predictions, and inference

emmeans — estimated marginal means, estimable functions, interaction contrasts, trends, and multiplicity adjustments.
marginaleffects — response-scale predictions, contrasts, slopes, and marginal standardization across model classes.
multcomp — simultaneous general linear hypotheses and multiplicity-adjusted confidence intervals/tests.



Diagnostics and influence

performance — standardized checks for singularity, convergence, collinearity, residual behavior, and overdispersion.
see — plotting backend used by performance::check_model() diagnostic panels.
DHARMa — simulation-based residual diagnostics for GLMMs, including dispersion and zero-inflation tests.
influence.ME — cluster-deletion influence measures and Cook’s distances for lme4 mixed models.
clubSandwich — cluster-robust covariance estimators and small-sample corrections for supported fitted-model classes.



Tidying and reproducible output

broom — tidy coefficient, fitted-value, and residual output for GLMs and many marginal models.
broom.mixed — tidy fixed effects, random effects, variance components, and confidence intervals from mixed models.
modelsummary — compact, reproducible comparison tables across supported model classes.

2. Model specification
For \(p\)-variate vectors \(Y_i\sim N_p(\mu_g,\Sigma)\), MANOVA tests \(H_0:C\mu=0\) using eigenvalues of \(E^{-1}H\) (Wilks, Pillai, Hotelling–Lawley, or Roy statistics). PCA diagonalizes the sample covariance/correlation matrix, \[

6. Extract & interpret
Pillai/Wilks tests address the joint sex difference across the four-age response vector; univariate follow-ups require multiplicity control and do not replace the joint test. PCA loadings define each linear combination, scores locate subjects, and \(\lambda_k/\sum\lambda_j\) is explained variance. Covariance PCA emphasizes occasions with larger variance; correlation PCA standardizes each occasion. Factor loadings represent a latent common-factor covariance model and are not PCA loadings. PCoA/MDS preserves pairwise distances rather than maximizing variance directly.

title: 8. Multivariate testing and PCA
text:
8. Caveats

Multivariate normality and common covariance are finite-sample assumptions for classical MANOVA; Pillai is often comparatively robust but not assumption-free.
A significant MANOVA does not identify which occasion or contrast drives the result.
PCA components are sample-dependent, sign-indeterminate, and unsupervised; selecting components by group separation leaks outcome information.
Complete-case wide matrices can discard substantial longitudinal information; LMM/GEE are preferable for irregular incomplete follow-up when the estimand is a trajectory effect.
PCA of repeated occasions mixes level and change; interpret loadings against the time ordering.
Source-backed: multivariate test statistics, PCA, factor analysis, PCoA, and MDS follow STAT 571. Standard-practice addition: the Orthodont reshaping makes all code self-contained.

title: 4. Marginal models and generalized estimating equations
text:
2. Model specification
Let \[
g(\mu_{ij})=x_{ij}^{\mathsf T}\beta,
\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=V_i=\phi A_i^{1/2}R_i(\alpha)A_i^{1/2}.
\] GEE solves \[
U(\beta)=\sum_{i=1}^m D_i^{\mathsf T}V_i^{-1}(Y_i-\mu_i)=0,
\qquad D_i=\frac{\partial\mu_i}{\partial\beta^{\mathsf T}}.
\] The model-based covariance is \(B^{-1}\); the sandwich covariance is \(B^{-1}MB^{-1}\), with \(B=\sum D_i^{\mathsf T}V_i^{-1}D_i\) and \(M=\sum D_i^{\mathsf T}V_i^{-1}r_ir_i^{\mathsf T}V_i^{-1}D_i\).

Time is the population-average weekly mean change in the reference feed group; Time:Cu terms are population-average differences in slopes. alpha parameterizes the chosen working correlation and is not ordinarily a scientific estimand in GEE1. For Gaussian data, \(\phi\) estimates residual scale; for binomial/Poisson responses the canonical scale is often fixed at one, although software can estimate a scale depending on options. Robust SEs come from vbeta; model-based SEs from vbeta.naiv are valid only under the working covariance model.
For nonidentity links, GEE and GLMM coefficients differ. With a logistic random-intercept GLMM, \[
\beta_{PA}\approx \frac{\beta_{SS}}{\sqrt{1+c^2\sigma_b^2}},
\qquad c=\frac{16\sqrt3}{15\pi}\approx0.588,
\] so population-averaged log-odds effects are typically attenuated toward zero. Under a probit link the corresponding factor is \((1+z_{ij}^{\mathsf T}Dz_{ij})^{-1/2}\); under the identity link the coefficients coincide.

title: 4. Marginal models and generalized estimating equations
text:
8. Caveats

GEE coefficients are population-averaged; GLMM coefficients are subject-specific conditional on random effects. Equality generally fails for nonidentity links.
Sandwich validity is asymptotic in the number of independent clusters; small-cluster corrections are not the default in geeglm().
Ordinary GEE is generally valid under MCAR, not arbitrary MAR dropout. Use weighted GEE or another valid missing-data method when observation depends on observed history.
geeglm() requires rows ordered by cluster and, for AR(1), correctly ordered waves.
Time-varying covariates can be external or endogenous; coefficients for endogenous covariates generally need a conditional/transition interpretation, and naive GEE can be biased when the covariate process depends on prior outcomes.
QIC is not AIC: it is based on quasi-likelihood and must be interpreted within comparable GEE specifications.
In geepack, vbeta is robust and vbeta.naiv is model-based. SAS/other R packages may label these empirical and model-based/naive; verify which covariance a printed table uses.
Scale estimation defaults differ across geepack, gee, and SAS PROC GENMOD/PROC GEE; set and report the rule explicitly.
Source-backed: estimating equations, sandwich inference, working correlations, QIC, scale, and PA interpretation follow the notes. Standard-practice addition: direct extraction helpers and emmeans::emtrends() are idiomatic R replacements for SAS contrasts.

2. Model specification
For descriptive purposes write \[
Y_{ij}=\mu_{G_i}(t_{ij})+\varepsilon_{ij},\qquad
\gamma(h)=\tfrac12 E\{(\varepsilon_i(t+h)-\varepsilon_i(t))^2\}.
\] The empirical variogram estimates \(\gamma(h)\); the time-indexed sample covariance matrix estimates \(\Sigma=(\sigma_{jk})\) only from subjects observed at the relevant pairs of occasions.

6. Extract & interpret
The spaghetti plot displays subject-level trajectory heterogeneity; the mean-profile interaction is read from nonparallel group curves, not from overlapping pointwise SE bands. Diagonal covariance entries are occasion-specific variances; off-diagonal entries and correlations summarize pairwise within-subject dependence. An increasing semivariogram indicates diminishing residual association with temporal separation. Pattern strings use 1 = observed, 0 = missing in increasing-age order.

8. Caveats

Pointwise SEs describe uncertainty in observed group means; they are not simultaneous bands and do not test a group-by-time interaction.
Pairwise covariance matrices under missingness can fail to be positive semidefinite because entries use different subject subsets.
A raw-response variogram confounds mean misspecification with dependence; compute it from residuals of a sufficiently rich mean model.
naniar is a visualization layer; mechanism labels (MCAR/MAR/MNAR) are assumptions, not identifiable from a missingness plot.

title: 6. Generalized linear mixed models
text:
2. Model specification
\[
g\{E(Y_{ij}\mid b_i)\}=x_{ij}^{\mathsf T}\beta+z_{ij}^{\mathsf T}b_i+log(e_{ij}),
\qquad b_i\sim N(0,D),
\] with conditional independence of \(Y_{ij}\) given \(b_i\). The marginal likelihood contribution is \[
L_i(\beta,D)=\int\left\{\prod_j f(y_{ij}\mid b_i;\beta)\right\}\phi(b_i;0,D)\,db_i.
\]

title: 6. Generalized linear mixed models
text:
8. Caveats

GEE is population-averaged; GLMM is subject-specific. Do not compare coefficient magnitudes without marginalization and link-specific attenuation.
glmer() uses Laplace at nAGQ = 1; nAGQ = 0 is a faster, less accurate approximation. Adaptive quadrature with nAGQ > 1 is restricted to a single scalar random-effect term.
SAS PROC GLIMMIX may default to pseudo-likelihood or different quadrature depending on options; match the estimation method explicitly before comparing results.
Overdispersion can reflect omitted random effects, serial dependence, zero inflation, or a wrong mean/variance family; a negative-binomial fit is not an automatic cure.
LRTs for random-effect variances have boundary nulls; plain chi-square p-values can be anticonservative.
Conditional modes are shrunken predictions and their empirical distribution is not a direct normality test of the latent population.
A transition-model coefficient conditions on observed response history and is neither a GEE marginal effect nor a random-effects subject-specific effect; initial-condition and missing-history handling must be stated.

text:
2. Model specification
Let \(R_{ij}=1\) indicate observation. Mechanisms are \[
\begin{aligned}
\text{MCAR: }&P(R\mid Y_{obs},Y_{mis},X)=P(R\mid X),\\
\text{MAR: }&P(R\mid Y_{obs},Y_{mis},X)=P(R\mid Y_{obs},X),\\
\text{MNAR: }&P(R\mid Y_{obs},Y_{mis},X)\text{ depends on }Y_{mis}.
\end{aligned}
\] MI combines \(m\) estimates with \[
\bar Q=m^{-1}\sum Q_k,\quad T=\bar U+(1+m^{-1})B.
\] For monotone dropout, IPW solves \(\sum_i D_i^{\mathsf T}V_i^{-1}W_i(Y_i-\mu_i)=0\), where \(W_i\) contains inverse estimated observation probabilities.

title: 7. Missing longitudinal data
text:
8. Caveats

MCAR/MAR/MNAR are statements about the joint full-data/observation process; observed data alone cannot distinguish MAR from MNAR.
Likelihood ignorability under MAR also requires distinct parameters and correct outcome modeling. MI requires congenial imputation/analysis models and inclusion of predictors of missingness and outcome.
LOCF treats an imputed value as known, distorts trajectories and covariance, and is generally unjustified except under a scientifically defensible constant-after-dropout estimand.
Standard mice wide imputation is appropriate for a modest common visit grid; irregular or multilevel data may require two-level methods (2l.pan, 2l.norm) or joint modeling.
Ordinary GEE is not generally valid under MAR dropout. IPW requires a correct observation model and positivity; weighted GEE scale and covariance defaults differ across R/SAS implementations.
Selection and pattern-mixture models are not identified under MNAR without restrictions. Report sensitivity parameters (e.g., delta adjustment/tipping point), not a single unverifiable fit.
EM maximizes the observed-data likelihood under its joint model; it does not by itself add between-imputation uncertainty or make an MNAR mechanism ignorable.
Source-backed: taxonomy, likelihood ignorability, MI, IPW, selection/pattern-mixture models, and LOCF limitations follow the notes. Standard-practice addition: mice/geepack code is the native R implementation.
